title: Northpeak Research x Redwood — Console + API demo (model versions & changelog feed)
summary: Northpeak requested a demo focused on (1) how Redwood exposes the *resolved* model version for requests (vs a moving alias like `rw/whatever-latest`) and (2) whether Redwood will provide a machine-readable model changelog feed (JSON/RSS) suitable for internal change-management workflows. Redwood walked through the planned model metadata schema + changelog pipeline: model registry as source of truth, signed change events, customer-safe templates, Console “Changelog” tab, and API/SDK surfaces (response fields/headers for resolved `model_version` + `changelog_url`). Northpeak asked about pagination, filtering, stability of IDs, ETags/caching, deprecation timelines, and how to avoid “silent” behavior changes during A/B tests and rollouts.
topics: Resolved model version in API responses and SDKs
Console UX: model page “Changelog” tab + exports
Rollouts/A-B tests and what customers will see
questions: Can we subscribe to updates programmatically (JSON feed) and store it in our own system of record?
Will the API response tell us exactly which version actually served the request (not just the alias)?
Do changelog entries have immutable IDs and are they tamper-evident?
Can we filter by model_id, date range, and change type (perf/compat/deprecation)?
Will you support ETags / If-None-Match for polling without rate issues?
How do you handle multiple changes in one day (ordering) and corrections to published notes?
next_steps: Redwood to share a draft of the public changelog feed contract (JSON shape, pagination, filters, ETag behavior).
Redwood to enable Northpeak in the Console changelog beta once the feature flag cohort opens.
Northpeak to send a sample of their internal change-management template (what fields they must capture) so Redwood can map required fields.
Schedule a 30-min follow-up: API headers/fields + SDK examples for resolved model versions (Python + TS).
action_items: Brian Murphy — Email Northpeak the proposed feed endpoint behavior (pagination + filters + ETags) and an example response — Due 2026-02-26
Monica Patel — Send SDK snippet showing how `model_version` and `changelog_url` surface in responses (Python + TS) — Due 2026-02-27
Quentin Harris — Confirm internal naming conventions for `model_id` / `version_id` that customers will see, and any redaction rules — Due 2026-02-27
Anika Rao — Share Northpeak’s compliance/change-management requirements for model changes (required fields, retention expectations) — Due 2026-02-28
transcript:
Fireflies.ai - Meeting Transcript

Title: Northpeak Research x Redwood — Console + API demo (model versions & changelog feed)
Date: 2026-02-22
Time: 4:00 PM - 4:46 PM PT
Duration: 46 min

Attendees:
- Brian Murphy (Redwood Inference)
- Monica Patel (Redwood Inference)
- Quentin Harris (Redwood Inference)
- Anika Rao (Northpeak Research)
- Jules Meyer (Northpeak Research)
- Samir Gupta (Northpeak Research)

---

Summary (auto-generated):
Customer requested machine readable release notes / changelog feed for model updates and asked for API exposure of resolved model versions. Redwood demoed early plan: model registry as source of truth, signed change events, console changelog tab, and API/SDK fields/headers that return model_version + changelog URL.

Topics (auto-generated):
- Model version pinning and resolved versions
- JSON feed / RSS feed for model updates
- Deprecations and change-management
- Console changelog tab

Action items (auto-generated):
- Redwood to share draft feed contract and example payload
- Redwood to share SDK examples for resolved version + changelog_url
- Customer to share internal change management requirements

---

[00:00] Brian Murphy: Alright, hey everyone. Thanks for making time. I’m Brian, I’m on the API surface side at Redwood. Monica’s here—she runs SDK—and Quentin from model catalog. Uh, the goal today is basically: show you what we’re building around model metadata and changelogs, and answer the questions you had about a machine-readable feed and… I think you called it “resolved model versions.”

[00:20] Anika Rao: Yep, that’s exactly it. We got burned recently with, not you specifically, but a provider where “latest” moved and nobody noticed until our evals flared. We want something we can ingest, like a JSON feed, and also something in the response so we can log what actually served.

[00:40] Brian Murphy: Makes sense. Before I share screen, quick context check: are you using hosted endpoints today anywhere or is this still evaluation?

[00:48] Samir Gupta: Evaluation. We have a small harness that can hit multiple vendors. We store prompts, outputs, and some tracing. But the weak link is the version metadata—like what model revision was actually used.

[01:03] Jules Meyer: Also we do a fair amount of A/B. If the provider is doing behind-the-scenes rollouts, we need some indicator or a changelog entry.

[01:15] Brian Murphy: Yep. So let me start with the “resolved version” concept. In Redwood, you can request a stable alias like, say, `rw/ember-3` or `rw/ember-3:stable`—naming is still being finalized—but under the hood it resolves to a specific version id. The thing you want is: every response includes that resolved `model_version`.

[01:35] Monica Patel: And in the SDKs, we’re planning to surface it as a first-class field, not something you have to dig out of headers only. But we can do both.

[01:44] Anika Rao: Both is good. Headers are nice because our gateway captures headers automatically.

[01:50] Brian Murphy: Right. So for OpenAI-compatible routes—like chat completions—we’re adding two things: a `model_version` field in the body (where possible without breaking compatibility), and a response header, something like `x-redwood-model-version`. Final name TBD but that’s the idea.

[02:10] Samir Gupta: Is that always present? Like streaming too?

[02:13] Brian Murphy: Good catch. For streaming, you still get response headers at the start of the stream, so you can grab it. And in the final “done” chunk we may also include it depending on format. But headers are the reliable part.

[02:28] Quentin Harris: Another point: the version id is intended to be immutable. Like `ember-3` could have versions `2026-02-10` and `2026-02-21` or a hash-style thing. We’re leaning toward a human-ish version id plus build metadata, but the customer-facing version won’t change once published.

[02:48] Jules Meyer: So if we pin, we’d pin the version id, not the alias.

[02:52] Brian Murphy: Exactly. Alias for convenience, version id for strict reproducibility.

[03:00] Anika Rao: And your routing? Like multi-region, fallback models—does that complicate it? Because if you fall back, we want to know.

[03:08] Brian Murphy: Yes, so the header would reflect the actual model+version served. If there’s fallback, it’ll be that fallback version. And the body can include both requested and resolved. Again, still finalizing exact shape.

[03:25] Monica Patel: We’re also adding a `changelog_url` alongside that, so you can click through or fetch the release note entry for that version.

[03:33] Samir Gupta: That’s huge. We could attach it to incident tickets.

[03:37] Brian Murphy: Cool. Now on the changelog feed. Quentin, do you want to tee up how we’re thinking about source-of-truth?

[03:45] Quentin Harris: Sure. Historically we had, like, docs pages and sometimes Slack messages. That doesn’t scale. So we’re making the model registry emit “change events” whenever metadata changes—create version, update compatibility notes, deprecate, etc. Those events are then used to generate customer-safe release notes.

[04:06] Anika Rao: Customer-safe meaning you redact internal stuff.

[04:09] Quentin Harris: Exactly. Like, we might have internal nicknames for a vendor model or kernel details. Those don’t go out. There’s an allowlist of fields that can appear in public changelog entries.

[04:22] Brian Murphy: Then we publish those as (1) a docs-site page and (2) a feed endpoint that’s JSON and cacheable.

[04:30] Anika Rao: The feed endpoint—this is what we care about. RSS is nice but our tooling is mostly JSON.

[04:36] Brian Murphy: Yep, same. The planned shape is something like: `GET /v1/changelog` with filters like `model_id=...` and date range and maybe `change_type`. Returns a list of entries with stable ids.

[04:52] Samir Gupta: Is it global or per-model?

[04:54] Brian Murphy: Both. Global feed for “all changes” and per-model. Like `GET /v1/models/{model_id}/changelog`. We’re still deciding whether we need both endpoints or one endpoint with filter.

[05:08] Jules Meyer: We’d prefer one with filters. Easier for us to implement.

[05:12] Brian Murphy: Noted.

[05:15] Anika Rao: And ETag support? So we can poll daily without downloading everything.

[05:20] Brian Murphy: Yes. ETags plus `If-None-Match`. Also probably `updated_at` cursor pagination. We’re sensitive to rate limiting so caching is part of the plan.

[05:36] Monica Patel: Also the SDKs might have a helper like `client.changelog.list(...)` but you can just hit HTTP.

[05:44] Samir Gupta: What about ordering guarantees? We’ve seen feeds where multiple updates in a day are not deterministic.

[05:52] Quentin Harris: We actually hit that in staging already. The plan is deterministic ordering by an event id that’s monotonic-ish (UUID plus timestamp). So if two updates happen same day, you can still sort by event id or published_at.

[06:12] Anika Rao: Great. Now one nuance: corrections. If you publish a release note and then realize wording is wrong, do you overwrite it? Because for audit we need to preserve.

[06:22] Brian Murphy: We won’t hard overwrite; we’ll do a superseding entry. Like, the original stays, marked as superseded, and the corrected one references it. That’s for auditability.

[06:35] Jules Meyer: That’s ideal.

[06:38] Brian Murphy: Let me show a quick mock in the Console, just so you see how it’s intended to look. (screen share)

[06:48] Brian Murphy: So here’s a model page—pretend this is `rw/ember-3`. You’ll see tabs: Overview, Metrics, Rollouts, and Changelog. In Changelog you get entries by version and by date. Each entry has: Summary, Impact, Compatibility, Deprecation if any, links to eval dashboards.

[07:12] Anika Rao: Links to eval dashboards—are those public?

[07:15] Quentin Harris: Mostly no, at least not initially. But we can link to a “customer-facing” metrics view in the Console for your account—like latency/throughput deltas. We’re trying to avoid exposing internal benchmark infra.

[07:30] Samir Gupta: That’s fine. For us, the key is just that there’s a pointer.

[07:35] Monica Patel: And from API side, you’d have `changelog_url` that points to a docs page or an API resource. We’re debating which is better long-term.

[07:46] Anika Rao: API resource preferred. Docs pages are okay but less stable for programmatic use.

[07:52] Brian Murphy: Yeah. We’re thinking the `changelog_url` could be an API URL, and docs site would render from the same published feed.

[08:05] Jules Meyer: How do you decide what constitutes a changelog-worthy event? Like, is a kernel upgrade a changelog entry?

[08:12] Quentin Harris: Great question. The schema captures both model version and runtime notes. For v1, if a runtime change materially affects perf or behavior for a specific model, we’ll cross-link it, but we might not do full narratives from eval diffs. More like “performance characteristics updated; see metrics.”

[08:33] Brian Murphy: So change types we’re using are roughly: “new model/version,” “performance,” “compatibility,” “deprecation,” “policy/safety,” and “bugfix.” Those labels may change.

[08:46] Anika Rao: For us, compatibility is big. Like tool calling, JSON mode, context window. We need those to not change silently.

[08:54] Quentin Harris: That’s explicitly in the metadata schema: context length, tool/function calling compatibility, structured output. If those fields change, it generates a changelog entry. And there will be a validation layer so required fields are present.

[09:12] Samir Gupta: Can you commit that a version’s metadata is immutable once published? Like context window doesn’t change.

[09:19] Quentin Harris: The *version* record should be immutable, yes. If we need to change something material, we publish a new version id. For purely descriptive metadata corrections, we’d use the superseding changelog mechanism, but the serving contract is: pinned versions are stable.

[09:38] Anika Rao: That’s the promise we need.

[09:41] Brian Murphy: Just to be transparent: there’s always the edge case where, like, a critical security issue forces an urgent patch. But even then, the goal is a new version id + an urgent changelog entry.

[09:55] Jules Meyer: Okay. What about A/B testing? If Redwood runs canaries on your side, does the customer see it?

[10:03] Brian Murphy: If you’re on a pinned version, we won’t canary you to a different version. If you’re on an alias that tracks “stable,” then yes, you might move as part of a rollout—BUT that would be paired with a published changelog entry and visible in rollouts history.

[10:22] Monica Patel: And we can expose a header that says you were served by variant A or B—this is more roadmap, not v1. But at minimum you’ll see resolved version.

[10:36] Samir Gupta: That’s fine, resolved version gets us most of the way.

[10:40] Anika Rao: Feed format questions. We need fields like: unique id, published timestamp, model id, version id, change type, summary, and a deprecation block with dates.

[10:54] Brian Murphy: Yup. Deprecation fields include: sunset date, replacement model/version, and customer messaging. Also a “last supported date” concept.

[11:06] Jules Meyer: And can we filter feed by change type? Like only deprecations.

[11:10] Brian Murphy: That’s planned. Either via query param `type=deprecation` or tags.

[11:17] Samir Gupta: Also retention—how far back will feed go? We might need a full export for audits.

[11:23] Quentin Harris: After migration, we’ll have full history going forward. Pre-migration, some historical notes will be incomplete. For enterprise, we can provide a backfilled “best effort” set for top models. But the canonical event log is retained internally with immutability guarantees.

[11:41] Anika Rao: “Best effort” is okay as long as going forward is solid.

[11:46] Brian Murphy: Makes sense.

[11:49] Monica Patel: On the SDK side, we’ll also keep these fields: `response.model`, `response.model_version`, `response.changelog_url`. So you can log them easily.

[12:00] Jules Meyer: Is that in both Python and TypeScript?

[12:03] Monica Patel: Yes. We’re aligning them.

[12:06] Brian Murphy: We should also talk about where this appears for OpenAI compatible responses. We can’t always add new top-level fields without breaking strict clients. But headers are safe. For the official Redwood SDK, we’ll give you structured fields.

[12:23] Samir Gupta: Great. We use the SDK in some places, and raw HTTP in others.

[12:29] Anika Rao: Another thing: do you have rate limits on the changelog feed? We’ll poll daily, maybe hourly if we’re nervous.

[12:36] Brian Murphy: There will be rate limits, but with ETag, hourly polling should be fine because most responses are 304. Also we can support “since” parameter.

[12:49] Quentin Harris: And the feed endpoint will be cached at edge with short TTL, plus ETag for correctness.

[12:57] Jules Meyer: Any chance of webhooks?

[13:00] Brian Murphy: Not in v1. We’re starting with batch/daily acceptable. Webhooks or streaming events later.

[13:09] Anika Rao: That’s okay. Daily is fine.

[13:12] Brian Murphy: Cool. Let’s do a quick walk through a hypothetical entry. Quentin, can you narrate what would show up?

[13:19] Quentin Harris: Sure. An entry would have something like:
- Title: “ember-3 version 2026-02-21 published”
- Summary: “Improved tool-calling reliability and reduced p95 latency in Hosted.”
- Impact: “No action required if pinned; aliases may update during rollout window.”
- Compatibility: “Context window unchanged: 128k. Tool calling: supported. Structured output: supported.”
- Deprecation: if applicable, “Previous version 2025-12-xx sunsets on … replacement is …”
- Links: “Console metrics dashboard” and “Docs reference.”

[13:58] Samir Gupta: That’s basically perfect.

[14:01] Jules Meyer: One concern: “improved tool calling” is vague. We’d want at least a hint of what changed.

[14:07] Quentin Harris: The style guide is to be customer-safe but informative. We can include “bugfix: fixed function call parsing for nested JSON arguments” if it’s accurate. But we avoid internal kernel or vendor details.

[14:22] Anika Rao: Right, don’t need vendor. Just need “what to expect.”

[14:27] Brian Murphy: Another question: do you want the feed to include performance deltas numbers?

[14:32] Anika Rao: Prefer links to metrics rather than hard-coded numbers. Numbers get out of date.

[14:38] Samir Gupta: Agree.

[14:41] Brian Murphy: Great.

[14:44] Monica Patel: Also, we can include a “breaking changes” boolean. If something is likely to impact prompts.

[14:51] Jules Meyer: Yeah, like changes in formatting or JSON output strictness.

[14:56] Quentin Harris: Exactly. We’ll treat those as “compatibility” changes with explicit notes.

[15:04] Brian Murphy: Okay. Let’s talk about your internal workflow. You said you want to ingest this into a system. Is it like a Slack bot, Jira, what?

[15:13] Anika Rao: We have an internal change-management log. It’s basically a service that watches vendor feeds and creates a ticket for the platform team to acknowledge. RSS works but JSON is better.

[15:27] Samir Gupta: We also store a snapshot of the entry for audit.

[15:31] Brian Murphy: Then you definitely want stable IDs and retention. Understood.

[15:37] Jules Meyer: Also, do you provide a way to export or download all entries?

[15:41] Brian Murphy: In the Console, there’ll be export. In API, you can page through everything. Might be “cursor” pagination.

[15:50] Anika Rao: Cursor is fine. But please document it well.

[15:54] Brian Murphy: Yeah. We will.

[15:57] Monica Patel: We’ve seen people struggle with “page=1” style for feeds. Cursor is safer.

[16:05] Samir Gupta: +1.

[16:07] Brian Murphy: Switching gears: competitors. You mentioned another provider. Are you comparing us to OpenAI direct, or open model hosts like Together?

[16:17] Anika Rao: Both. OpenAI is easy but we can’t get the level of control we want. Together and Fireworks have some versioning but not a real changelog feed. At least not in the format we need.

[16:34] Brian Murphy: Okay. So if we deliver the feed + resolved version, that’s a major differentiator for you.

[16:40] Anika Rao: Yes.

[16:41] Jules Meyer: Also dedicated vs hosted. If we go dedicated, does the changelog still apply? Or is it separate.

[16:48] Quentin Harris: It applies across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. That’s the point: same schema and same changelog mechanism. Some entries will note “Hosted only” or “Dedicated only” changes.

[17:05] Samir Gupta: For Private, you’d have to publish it differently though.

[17:09] Quentin Harris: Private may have a private control plane endpoint. But the entry format is consistent.

[17:16] Anika Rao: Great.

[17:18] Brian Murphy: Let’s hit the concrete asks: you want (1) resolved version in API responses, (2) a machine-readable changelog feed with ETags, filters, stable IDs, and (3) a `changelog_url` that points to the entry.

[17:33] Anika Rao: Yes.

[17:35] Brian Murphy: Anything else?

[17:37] Jules Meyer: A deprecation timeline policy. Like minimum notice.

[17:41] Quentin Harris: Policy is being standardized. For major deprecations, we target 60–90 days notice depending on tier, with explicit “sunset date” and replacement. For urgent security issues, it can be shorter but still documented.

[17:58] Anika Rao: As long as it’s explicit.

[18:00] Samir Gupta: And if we’re pinned, we can ride it until sunset.

[18:04] Quentin Harris: Correct.

[18:06] Brian Murphy: Let’s talk about the feed contract a bit more. Would you prefer the entry includes the full body text, or just pointers?

[18:14] Anika Rao: Full text in feed. Pointers too, but full text makes the archive easy.

[18:19] Brian Murphy: Okay, so the JSON entry includes fields like `title`, `summary`, `impact`, `compatibility_notes`, `deprecation`, etc.

[18:31] Samir Gupta: And would there be a signature? Like tamper evidence.

[18:35] Brian Murphy: We’re considering signed change events internally. For the public feed, we at least have immutable IDs and audit logs. We can talk to security about exposing a signature. Might be overkill for v1 but I get the ask.

[18:52] Anika Rao: Not required day one, but good to know.

[18:56] Monica Patel: Most customers solve it by snapshotting and storing hash on their side.

[19:02] Samir Gupta: Yep.

[19:04] Brian Murphy: Another nuance: do you want separate feeds per environment? Like Hosted vs Dedicated.

[19:11] Anika Rao: Filter is fine. Like `deployment=hosted`.

[19:15] Brian Murphy: We can add that.

[19:18] Quentin Harris: In schema, versions can indicate availability by deployment mode, so feed can include that as a tag.

[19:28] Jules Meyer: Perfect.

[19:30] Brian Murphy: Okay. Let’s do a Q&A open floor.

[19:34] Anika Rao: What’s the timeline? When can we use the feed?

[19:39] Brian Murphy: We’re targeting a beta in the next few weeks. I don’t want to overpromise. But there’s active work: schema, migration, generator, console integration, and API surface.

[19:53] Monica Patel: SDK exposure should land around the same window as the API headers, because we need the backend to provide the fields.

[20:01] Anika Rao: Could we be in the beta cohort?

[20:03] Brian Murphy: Yes, that’s why we wanted to meet. We can flag your account.

[20:08] Samir Gupta: Great.

[20:10] Jules Meyer: Another question: if we call the model via OpenAI compatible endpoint, will the response `model` field include the alias or the version?

[20:18] Brian Murphy: The `model` field typically reflects what you requested, for compatibility. But we can include the resolved version via header and possibly in a `usage` extension. Again, we need to be careful not to break clients.

[20:35] Jules Meyer: Understood.

[20:37] Monica Patel: The Redwood SDK can return both: requested_model and resolved_model_version.

[20:43] Anika Rao: Great.

[20:45] Samir Gupta: One more. Is the changelog entry tied to a rollout? Like if the alias moved, will you show the exact time window.

[20:53] Quentin Harris: Changelog entry is per version change event and publication time. Rollouts show when traffic shifted. We’ll cross-link: rollouts page points to the published changelog entry that corresponds to that version.

[21:10] Samir Gupta: That is exactly what we want for incident analysis.

[21:13] Brian Murphy: Cool.

[21:15] Anika Rao: Okay, slightly paranoid question: can internal people edit metadata after the fact? Like change context window in metadata without changing version.

[21:25] Quentin Harris: We’re implementing RBAC and audit events. Certain fields are immutable post-publish. Others are editable but would emit a change event and a corrected changelog entry. The serving contract should not change for pinned versions.

[21:43] Anika Rao: Good.

[21:45] Monica Patel: And our docs team is adding linting to prevent internal-only fields from leaking.

[21:50] Jules Meyer: Nice.

[21:52] Brian Murphy: I think we’ve covered the big topics. Let’s confirm what you need from us to proceed.

[22:00] Anika Rao: If you can share the proposed JSON schema for the feed—like an example payload—that would unblock our integration planning.

[22:10] Samir Gupta: And the exact response header name for resolved model version, so we can update our gateway logging. Even if it’s “subject to change,” we can start.

[22:20] Brian Murphy: We can share a draft and then lock it before beta.

[22:24] Monica Patel: I’ll send SDK snippets too.

[22:27] Jules Meyer: Great.

[22:29] Brian Murphy: Anything else? Maybe you can share your internal ticket template so we ensure we have all fields.

[22:36] Anika Rao: Yep. We can share a redacted template.

[22:40] Brian Murphy: Perfect.

[22:42] (crosstalk)

[22:43] Samir Gupta: Sorry quick last thing—does feed include “known issues”?

[22:49] Quentin Harris: There’s a support-facing doc for known gaps, but customer-facing entries can include “known issues” section when relevant, yes. We’re careful with wording.

[23:01] Samir Gupta: That’s helpful.

[23:03] Brian Murphy: Alright. I’ll stop the screen share.

[23:07] Brian Murphy: Recap: we’ll email you the draft feed contract + example; Monica will send SDK examples; we’ll add you to the beta list; you’ll send the change-management requirements template.

[23:22] Anika Rao: Sounds good.

[23:24] Jules Meyer: Thanks.

[23:25] Samir Gupta: Thanks everyone.

[23:28] Brian Murphy: Cool. Talk soon.

(Transcript ends — recording continued with silence)

[23:45] Fireflies.ai note: Meeting ended at 46:02 (some audio not transcribed).
